newsitem.title: USA: AFL-CIO opposed to WTO membership for China.
newsitem.headline: AFL-CIO opposed to WTO membership for China.

text.p: The head of the AFL-CIO said Wednesday the labor group opposed granting China early admission into the World Trade Organization until it reforms its policies toward free trade and worker rights.
In remarks to a trade conference, AFl-CIO President John Sweeney said unions operating in Hong Kong are at risk as China moves to take over the colony June 30.

"Favored access to our market and admission to the WTO should be dependent upon its playing by the same rules as other nations, and conditioned on the guarantee of basic human rights, including the rights of workers to organize, bargain and to strike," he said.
Sweeney, who just returned from a trip to Honk Kong, said that while private enterprise may be protected, restrictions are already being imposed on speech, assembly and the press.
"Honk Kong's free trade unions, weakened by export of jobs to China, are at the greatest risk as China takes over," he told the trade conference sponsored by the Economic Strategy Institute.
Sweeney said it was troubling that Vice President Al Gore and House Speaker Newt Gingrich made no mention of those unions as a measure of democratic freedom in their recent trips to Asia.
"Too often, American leaders assume that the spread of markets alone will bring the spread of democracy," he said.

Sweeney also said his union will oppose renewing China's most favored nation (MFN) trade status. President Clinton has until June to decide whether to renew MFN, which gives China the same access to U.S. markets as most other trading nations. Congress then must decide whether to accept MFN renewal or vote to revoke it.

White House officials have said they expect Clinton to renew China's MFN status. Many trade analysts have said they expect a tough fight in Congress because of concerns about human rights abuses, nuclear techonology sales and allegations that Beijing tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.
House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt told the group he will probably oppose renewal of China's MFN status this year, as he did last year.
But Boeing Co. Chairman Philip Condit told the conference that failure to renew China's trade status would have a severe impact on Boeing sales.

Lawmakers are also concerned about the ballooning U.S. trade deficit with China, which hit nearly $40 billion last year, up from about $34 billion in 1995, and is the second largest U.S. trade deficit after that with Japan.

Sun Zhenyu, vice minister of China's Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the conference that Beijing was sensitive to U.S. concerns about the trade gap and was looking to boost U.S. imports.
"Of course, we recognize the trade deficit issue is of great concern in this country," Sun said. "We shall work very closely with our U.S. counterparts to promote U.S. exports to China," he said.
He did not address human rights concerns.
